transcript.text: smelt burning plastic and saw a wisp of smoke from the top of the dishwasher door, the lights went off. I've switched it off at the wall. can I just try it again?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
A burning smell or smoke can mean an electrical fault or a fire risk. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it (or turn it off at the fuse box), and don't run it again — not even as a test — until it has been checked by a qualified engineer. No, please do not try it again. A burning plastic smell and smoke from the door area suggests an electrical component (like the control board, wiring, or heating element) has overheated or failed. The lights going off may indicate a trip or a short circuit. Since this involves mains electricity and potential fire risk, you must leave the appliance switched off at the wall and unplugged. I need to know if there is any water in the bottom of the machine or if the filter is blocked, as this can sometimes lead to leaks that cause electrical shorts. Please check for standing water and a blocked filter while it remains isolated.

It's already switched off at the fused spur on the wall. I haven't looked for water inside and I'd rather not open the door again after the smoke. There's a brown scorch mark on the top edge of the control strip near the buttons. Is that enough to say I shouldn't use it?

⚠ Stop using this appliance
Yes, that is absolutely enough reason not to use it again. The combination of burning plastic smell, smoke, lights going off (likely a trip), and now a visible scorch mark on the control strip strongly points to an electrical short circuit or melted insulation within the control panel area. This is a fire risk and involves mains voltage. Please leave the appliance switched off at the wall and do not attempt to open it yourself. You will need to call a qualified engineer to inspect and repair the internal wiring or control board.
